content.text: I'll look through the event-handler wiring to see why detach and re-attach duplicates webhooks, audit rows, and usage counts while leaving in-app notifications alone.

content.thinking:
The bug is in the event bus's `subscribe` function.

The unsubscribe function deletes the handler from a stale copy of the handler set instead of the current set stored in `handlers`.

Each new subscription copies the old handler set into a fresh Set and stores it in the map. The unsubscribe function deletes from its own stale copy, so the handler is never removed from the current map entry.

The stale unsubscribe leaves the handler attached to the current map entry. Re-registering adds new handlers while the old ones remain, so duplicates accumulate across cycles. This matches the reported duplication of webhooks, audit log, and usage counter.

In-app notifications were never duplicated. They attach on first import and have no register entry point, so they remain unaffected by the event bus bug. The event registry's register and unregister logic is correct: it tracks detach state and stays idempotent. Notifications must keep being delivered exactly once throughout, including while other handlers are detached.

The fix must remove handlers from the live map entry rather than from a stale snapshot. The copy-on-write design was meant to prevent mutation during event emission, but it causes unsubscribe to delete from the wrong set.

The copy-on-write design is intentional to keep event emission stable. The fix is to have the unsubscribe function look up the current live handler set from the map at runtime instead of deleting from its own stale snapshot.

Two implementation paths are being weighed. One creates a fresh Set from the live map entry and stores it back after deletion. The other mutates the current Set directly. The direct mutation risks breaking emit's iteration if it runs concurrently.

Extending copy-on-write to unsubscribe would keep in-flight emits safe. Each unsubscribe would create a fresh set without the handler and store it, so the current emit continues iterating the old set while future emits use the updated one. A subtle race remains if two unsubscribes happen concurrently.

A race condition exists if two unsubscribes read the same live handler set before either writes back. The second unsubscribe would then delete a handler that the first already removed, restoring it to the map. Because JavaScript is single-threaded and these operations are synchronous, this race cannot occur in practice. The proposed fix reads the current set at runtime, creates a fresh copy, deletes the handler from that copy, and stores the updated set back.

A simpler alternative to copy-on-write is being considered. Instead of copying the handler set on every subscription, the code could keep one mutable Set and only create a snapshot when emitting events. This would eliminate the stale-set problem entirely while still protecting in-flight iterations.

The simpler mutable-set approach is rejected because the current subscribe function closes over a fresh handler set on every call. Fixing only the unsubscribe would still leave the live map entry untouched. The fix must update the live set directly in the map. The subscribeOnce implementation is now being examined.

content.thinking:
The bug is confirmed. The `subscribe` function uses copy-on-write.

The unsubscribe function deletes the handler from the stale copied Set. The live Set remains unchanged.

This explains why the bug only surfaces after detach and reattach. Notification handlers are registered at module load before other listeners, so they become the first subscribers. When activity, webhook, or usage handlers subscribe later to the same events, they copy the Set that still contains those notification handlers. Those notification handlers are never unsubscribed.

Notification handlers are never detached, so they stay registered permanently. Webhook, audit, and usage handlers are the ones actually duplicating. Multiple services subscribe to the same events, and only the last subscriber's unsubscribe removes from the live Set. Earlier subscribers delete from stale copies instead. On re-register, new handlers stack on top of those stale entries.

A concrete trace of `issue.created` shows the exact cascade. Activity registers first, then search copies that Set, then usage copies both activity and search, then webhook copies all three. When unregistering in reverse order, each handler deletes from its own stale copy. The live Set retains every handler.

The trace shows only three handlers remain after one unregister, not seven. This contradicts the user's report of two or three duplicates. The exact duplication count needs re-examination.

The user's reports of duplicate audit logs and double issue counts suggest the duplication is more severe than the trace indicates. If webhook were always the last subscriber, it should survive a single detach-and-reattach cycle cleanly. The fact that it does not suggests either webhook is not consistently last, or multiple webhook subscriptions are interacting in unexpected ways.

The webhook listener subscribes to `issue.created` last. Its unsubscribe removes only that handler from the live Set, leaving activity, search, and usage intact. Re-registering then stacks all four handlers on top of the existing ones.

The trace suggests webhook deliveries should remain single and only audit and usage would double. Yet the user reports webhooks themselves are duplicated two or three times. The webhook service subscribes to `issue.created` before `issue.status_changed`, so nothing else registers for that event afterward. This leaves the reported duplication count unexplained.

A second detach-and-reattach cycle stacks all four handlers again. The live Set now holds eight entries: the original three plus four new ones. The first unsubscribe still only removes the oldest handler from its stale copy, leaving the rest intact.

The second detach-and-reattach cycle removes the newest webhook handler from the live Set. The old webhook handler is already gone from its stale copy. Only the original activity, search, and usage handlers remain in the live Set. Re-registering then adds four fresh handlers on top of those three. Webhooks should therefore appear once per cycle. This still does not explain why the user sees webhooks duplicated two or three times.

The trace still shows webhooks should remain single, which conflicts with the user's report of duplicates. I am now checking whether the last subscriber's unsubscribe fails in some cases, or if handler functions are somehow being registered twice. Since each subscribe call creates a new arrow function, Set deduplication by reference rules out duplicate handlers.

I am now examining whether the register functions themselves contain a bug that prevents combined unsubscription from working correctly. I am also investigating Next.js hot reload behavior: if the event-registry module is re-evaluated, its detach state resets to null, but the event-bus handlers map might persist if that module is not reloaded.

Only the webhook subscriber actually removes its handler during detach. Activity, search, and usage remain in the live set. After one cycle, those three have two handlers each while webhook has one. The user's report of webhooks duplicating two or three times likely reflects repeated hot reload cycles.

A step-by-step simulation of two full cycles shows the live handler set never shrinks. After the first unregister, only the webhook subscriber is removed, leaving activity, search, and usage intact. The next register then adds fresh handlers to that same persistent set, so duplicates accumulate with every cycle.

The simulation shows webhooks should stay at one handler forever if they are always the last subscriber. The user reports they duplicate, so the detach logic must be removing them after all. The real cause is still unknown.

The registration order is now being re-examined. The list shows activity, search, usage, and webhook listeners registered in sequence, so the assumption that webhook always subscribes last may be wrong. If another subscriber registers after webhook, or if the unsubscribe logic fails for the final handler, that would explain the duplication. Another possibility is that a separate trigger mechanism is causing the repeated deliveries.

The investigation now suspects the copy-on-write logic itself is broken. If the unsubscribe step deletes from a copied set while the live set remains the original, handlers would persist in the live set and duplicate on every reload.

The copy-on-write theory is ruled out. The subscribe function copies the handler set before adding, so the unsubscribe callback removes from the copied set. The investigation now turns to whether unregister runs in reverse order.

Checking the subscribers for issue status changes.

Only activity-service and webhook-service subscribe to issue.status_changed. Activity registers first, then webhook. During unregistration, activity removes from its stale set while webhook removes from its live set. After one cycle, activity remains but webhook is gone. Re-registering causes activity to duplicate while webhook stays single.

The duplication might instead come from copy-on-write semantics. Unsubscribe could delete from a stale set while emit reads from the live one, so removing an earlier handler leaves duplicates behind.

The copy-on-write theory is unlikely because the webhook handler is last and should not leak. The focus shifts to Next.js hot reload: if the event-registry module reloads while the event-bus stays cached, detach becomes null and register could fire again without deduplication.

The notification-service module uses an import-time guard that resets on reload. This would duplicate notification handlers if the module reloaded. The user reports notifications were never duplicated, so this path is ruled out.

Notification handlers surviving prove modules are not fully reloaded. The detach flag persists, so register would exit early and avoid duplication. The ops button explicitly detaches and reattaches handlers, which is the actual trigger.

The detach function fails to fully remove handlers because of the stale set bug. Activity leaks while webhook unsubscribes correctly. That would leave one webhook and two audits, not the reported two or three duplicates.

Import order may explain the webhook duplication. notification-service subscribes to comment.created at module import time, before registerEventHandlers runs. This means notification handlers are registered before the event-registry attaches its own listeners.

Examining the activity test around line 135, specifically the "sibling" handler.

The stale-set bug theory doesn't explain the webhook duplication. Webhooks are last subscribers and shouldn't leak, yet they duplicate while notifications don't. Either another bug exists or the registration order differs in the failing scenario.

Re-examined the subscribe code. The closure captures the live Set, so unsubscribing removes the handler correctly. Webhooks should not leak. This contradicts the user's report.

A Next.js HMR module re-evaluation scenario was considered. If the module is disposed and then re-evaluated, the stored detach may not run. The new module would register all handlers again. Webhook count would still be one. This does not explain the duplicates.

A new theory explains the duplication pattern. If HMR preserves the event-bus module but re-executes the event-registry, the stored detach becomes null and registerEventHandlers adds a second handler set.
